changes.text: + challenge: Extra capacity may be taken up by the jobs currently being turned away, leaving the wait for each customer much the same.

changes.text: + challenge: Finding a mechanic and getting them up to speed takes time, so the effect on the wait by the end of March may be smaller than the extra hours suggest.
changes.detail: Finding a mechanic and getting them up to speed takes time, so the effect on the wait by the end of March may be smaller than the extra hours suggest. · challenge · Proposed by Olumi: New hires rarely work at full pace from the first week, and the deadline is fixed.

changes.text: + challenge: Stopping e-bike work gives up the income and the customers those jobs bring, and neither aim would show that loss.

chat.said: Our bike repair workshop turns away about 12 repair jobs a week because both mechanics are fully booked. We want the average wait for a repair under 5 days by the end of March, and we can't spend more than £1,500 a month extra. We could hire a part-time mechanic for about £1,300 a month, open on Sundays, or stop taking e-bike jobs, which take roughly twice as long as ordinary ones. Jo thinks Sunday opening would only spread the same work over more days. The average wait is about 9 days now.

answer.text: The part-time hire is the only option with a real chance on the wait aim, and it hinges on Olumi's estimate of how much each extra mechanic hour shortens the wait.

why.text: If Olumi's estimates hold, the hire's chance swings from about 71% if 'Effect of each extra hours/week on average wait for a repair' is low, about 4% if it is high, so this one figure largely decides it.
The hire fits your spending limit at about 98% (of staying within Extra spend no more than £1,500 a month) (if Olumi's estimates hold), yet

why.cite: With every figure at its most likely value and no risk happening, 'Hire a part-time mechanic', for 'Average repair wait under 5 days by end of March': 'average wait for a repair' 5.61 days, against a target of less than 5 days: misses it. It rests on Olumi's what-if ranges for 'Mechanic hours worked in the workshop changed: Hire a part-time mechanic' (12 to 24 hours/week), 'Effect of each extra hours/week on average wait for a repair' (−0.3 to −0.1 days weeks/hours). It reads their approximate 'Current average wait for a repair' as 10% either way, 8 times in 10, until they give a range.

why.text: shows it missing on middle figures.

text.text: What have you seen, such as weeks with extra cover, showing how much one added hour shortens your queue?
